questions.question: What is the key difference between a local and a remote (push) notification?
options: Local notifications require a backend server; remote notifications do not
Local notifications are scheduled entirely on-device with no server involved; remote notifications are sent from a server through a push service like APNs/FCM
There is no real difference, both terms describe the same mechanism
Remote notifications only work when the app is open
questions.explanation: A local notification is purely a device-side timer; a remote notification requires a backend, a push service, and network delivery to reach the device.

questions.question: What is a device push token, and why does your backend need it?
options: A password the user enters to enable notifications
A unique identifier for a specific app install on a specific device, obtained from FCM/APNs, which the backend needs to target that device when sending a push
An encryption key used only for local notifications
A setting stored only in the app's local storage, never sent anywhere
questions.explanation: The backend uses the device's token to tell the push service (FCM/APNs) exactly which installed app instance should receive a given notification.

questions.question: Why do production apps need to handle token-refresh events, not just the initial token fetch?
options: Tokens expire every few seconds and must be constantly polled
A device's push token can change (e.g. after reinstall or an OS-level refresh), and failing to re-send the new token means notifications silently stop reaching that device
Token refresh is only relevant for local notifications
It's purely optional and has no real consequence if skipped
questions.explanation: If the backend keeps using a stale token after it's rotated, push sends to that user will fail without any obvious error on the client side.

questions.question: Why do iOS and Android both restrict what an app can do while running in the background?
options: It's a React Native-specific limitation that doesn't apply to native apps
It's deliberate platform policy primarily aimed at preserving battery life, not a framework limitation
Background execution is technically impossible on mobile hardware
Only Android restricts background work; iOS has no such restrictions
questions.explanation: Both platforms intentionally limit background execution for battery and resource reasons, and this applies equally regardless of whether the app is built natively or with React Native.
